# Introduction

# **Metawatt Internship Guidebook**

Welcome to the Metawatt Internship Guidebook\!

This guide is designed to help you make the most out of your internship experience. Here, you’ll find everything you need to get started with daily protocols, team structure, key personnel and their roles, internship timelines, and important expectations.

We encourage you to refer back to this guide whenever needed as you progress through the program.

## **What Metawatt Is**

Metawatt is an AI-focused platform that provides hands-on learning experiences through real-world projects and practical training. It aims to bridge the gap between academic knowledge and industry application by giving learners access to tools, mentorship, and project-based work in artificial intelligence and related fields.

Rather than focusing solely on theory, Metawatt emphasizes experiential learning for interns to actively build, test, and deploy solutions in realistic scenarios.

## **What We Do at Metawatt**

At Metawatt, we design and develop AI-driven solutions while training individuals to become industry-ready professionals. Our work involves applying artificial intelligence, data analysis, and automation to solve real-world problems.

As an intern, you can expect to:

* Work on real or simulated industry projects  
* Collaborate with mentors and fellow interns  
* Gain exposure to modern AI tools and workflows  
* Develop both technical and professional skills

The internship is structured to provide a strong foundation for your future career.

## **Metawatt’s Vision and Mission**

**Vision**

To cultivate a generation of innovators equipped with the skills and mindset to shape the future through artificial intelligence.

**Mission**

* To provide accessible, hands-on learning in AI and emerging technologies  
* To bridge the gap between education and industry through real-world experience  
* To empower individuals with practical, job-ready skills  
* To foster a collaborative environment that encourages innovation and growth

# Surplus Funds

# **Surplus Funds**

Surplus Funds is a Metawatt project developed to help individuals from the US recover surplus funds from counties.

## **What are surplus funds?**

Surplus funds is money owed to individuals from an excess of a bidding in an auction. But how does this even happen in the first place? When individuals fail to pay their taxes, their property gets auctioned off by their county to cover the cost. In an auction, the final bid may be higher than the properties’ actual value. The county will only take what’s owed to them. So if the original value was around $2,500 and the final bid is $4,000, the county will only take the $2,500 while the remaining $1,500 just sits in the treasury. That excess amount is referred to as “Surplus Funds” and it is legally owed back to the owner of the property.   
![graph TD    %% Define styles    classDef action fill:\#f8f9fa,stroke:\#6c757d,stroke-width:2px,color:black;    classDef county fill:\#f8d7da,stroke:\#dc3545,stroke-width:2px,color:black;    classDef money fill:\#d4edda,stroke:\#28a745,stroke-width:2px,color:black;    classDef surplus fill:\#fff3cd,stroke:\#ffc107,stroke-width:3px,color:black;    classDef owner fill:\#cce5ff,stroke:\#007bff,stroke-width:2px,color:black;    %% The Event Flow    A\[Property Owner\]:::owner --\>|"Fails to pay taxes"| B\[County Auctions Property\]:::action        %% The Auction Math    B --\>|"Auction concludes"| C{Final Bid: $4,000}:::money        %% The Split    C --\>|"Covers taxes & costs"| D\[County takes what is owed: $2,500\]:::county    C ==\>|"Excess from bidding"| E((Surplus Funds: $1,500)):::surplus        %% The Result    E --\>|"Sits safely in"| F\[County Treasury\]:::county    E -.-\>|"Legally owed back to"| A][image1]  
*Figure 1: Flow diagram of how surplus funds are generated*

## **The problem**

The county will keep the surplus funds safe but will not make an effort to contact the property owner properly. Some counties do send a letter to the property addressed to the previous property owner but most individuals aren’t even aware of the concept of surplus funds so they almost never even thought of checking. Some counties are also incentivized to not make an effort due to local law allowing surplus funds to be absorbed into government funds after some time has passed. Essentially, many individuals in the US aren’t aware that they have money legally owed to them just sitting in county treasuries. 

![sequenceDiagram    autonumber    participant Gov as Local Government    participant County as County Treasury    participant Owner as Property Owner    rect rgb(255, 235, 235)    Note over Gov, Owner: PART 1: The Trap (Status Quo Problem)        County-\>\>County: Holds funds safely ($1,500)    County-.-\>Owner: Sends minimal, ineffective notice\<br/\>(e.g., letter to old address)        Note over Owner: Unaware of surplus funds concept.\<br/\>Does not check for them.        opt If extensive time passes (Local Law)        County-\>\>Gov: Funds legally absorbed into government accounts    end    end][image2]  
*Figure 2: Sequence diagram of what happens after the auction.*

Retrieving the surplus funds is also not as straightforward as going into one’s local county and asking for it directly. It needs to go through a legal process with an attorney. This requires paper work and many months before the request to retrieve the surplus funds is processed.

There already exist individuals and groups performing surplus funds acquisition as a job. Their role is to reach out to individuals and inform them of their surplus funds. They then ask the client to entrust them with retrieving their surplus funds for a commission rate. For example, if the surplus funds is $1,500 and the commission rate is 30%, then they get $450 for that commission.

![sequenceDiagram    autonumber    participant Owner as Property Owner    participant Acquirer as Surplus Funds Acquirer    participant Legal as Attorney / Legal Process    participant County as County Treasury    rect rgb(235, 245, 255)    Note over Owner, County: PART 2: The Retrieval (Business Model Solution)        Acquirer-\>\>Owner: Proactively reaches out and informs them of owed money    Note over Owner: Cannot simply ask County for it.        Owner-\>\>Acquirer: Signs retrieval contract & 30% commission agreement        Acquirer-\>\>Legal: Initiates strict formal legal process    Legal-\>\>County: Submits complete legal paperwork    Note over Legal, County: Processing takes many months        County-\>\>Legal: Approves request and releases funds        par Retrieval Payout Distribution        Legal-\>\>Owner: Transfers remaining funds (e.g., $1,050 / 70%)    and        Legal-\>\>Acquirer: Pays out commission (e.g., $450 / 30%)    end    end][image3]  
*Figure 3: Sequence diagram of how surplus funds retrieval works*

## **How does Surplus Funds Acquisition work?**

There exists 3 phases for Surplus Funds Acquisition (SFA): Client Acquisition, Closing, and lastly Fulfillment. Client Acquisition (CA) is where clients are acquired through outbound calls or cold calling.This is usually done after collecting all required information about the client through a process called skip tracing. Skip tracing usually starts at the auction details which are commonly found in county websites. Client details are extracted from there which include their full name, contact details, surplus funds, and many more. The SFA agent starts CA by contacting the client via all possible channels; and if it doesn’t work then they will proceed with contacting their relatives. Once CA is successful, the process moves to phase 2: Closing.

Closing involves informing the client about their surplus funds with the goal of getting them to sign an agreement for retrieving the surplus funds. This involves careful handling to ensure that the client does not think that the whole process is sketchy. From their perspective, there’s no such thing as free lunch, so what’s the catch? But for surplus funds, there is no catch. Just the long arduous process of handling legal requirements meant for the legal team to process. 

Once the client has locked in, it’s time to move to the last phase: Fulfilment. Legal processes take place in this phase. Most of the process is attorneys asking for documents from the clients, and the clients asking for updates regarding the acquisition. Once everything has been handled, money is handed over to the client, and the SFA agent takes a cut of that surplus funds as per the deal. Rinse and repeat.

![graph TD    %% Phase 1: Client Acquisition    subgraph Phase1 \[Phase 1: Client Acquisition\]        CW\[(County Websites)\] --\> AD\[/Auction Details/\]        AD --\> ST\[Process: Skip Tracing\]        ST --\> CD\[/Data Extracted: Full Name, Contact, Surplus Amount/\]        CD --\> OC\[Action: Outbound / Cold Calling\]        OC --\> Reached{Client Contacted?}        Reached -- No --\> CR\[Action: Contact Relatives\]        CR --\> Reached        Reached -- Yes --\> EndP1(\[Phase 1 Complete\])    end    %% Phase 2: Closing    subgraph Phase2 \[Phase 2: Closing\]        EndP1 --\> IC\[Inform Client of Surplus Funds\]        IC --\> HS\[Address Skepticism / Explain 'No Catch'\]        HS --\> Explain\[Explain Arduous Legal Process Ahead\]        Explain --\> Sign{Agreement Signed?}        Sign -- No --\> IC        Sign -- Yes --\> EndP2(\[Phase 2 Complete\])    end    %% Phase 3: Fulfillment    subgraph Phase3 \[Phase 3: Fulfillment\]        EndP2 --\> LP{{Legal Processes Commenced}}        LP --\> Docs\[/Attorneys Request Documents/\]        Docs --\> Updates\[/Client Requests Updates/\]        Updates --\> Handled{Legal Process Complete?}        Handled -- No --\> LP        Handled -- Yes --\> Money\[/Money Handed to Client/\]        Money --\> Cut\[SFA Agent Takes Contractual Cut\]    end    %% Loop    Cut --\> Repeat(\[Rinse and Repeat\])    Repeat -.-\> CW    %% Styling    style Phase1 fill:\#f9f9f9,stroke:\#333,stroke-width:2px    style Phase2 fill:\#f0f4ff,stroke:\#333,stroke-width:2px    style Phase3 fill:\#f9fff0,stroke:\#333,stroke-width:2px        style Reached fill:\#fff4dd    style Sign fill:\#fff4dd    style Handled fill:\#fff4dd        style CW fill:\#e1f5fe    style LP fill:\#f3e5f5][image4]

*Figure 4\. Phases of Surplus Funds Acquisition*

## **Where we come in**

The weakness of current traditional methods is manual labor. It is not scalable.They are limited by the amount of hands they have. Metawatt devises a solution: to automate client acquisition with the use of AI tools and web scrapers. Metawatt envisions an application that uses AI tools to reach out to clients, handle closing, and assist with the legal processes. With tools like Retell AI, DropCowboy, GoHighLevel, and ElevenLabs, client outreach has never been this automatic. This application can scale to reach several states at once compared to manual labor; giving Metawatt a huge advantage compared to existing competition.

# System Details

# **System Details**

The surplus system consists of 4 components: The Agentic RAG/Knowledge Base (RAG/KB), Web Scraping (WS), GoHighLevel (GHL), and API & Database (AND) components. Each component plays a critical role in the business operations. 

The WS component handles skip tracing i.e. collecting client data from each county’s auction. The data is then handed over to the AND component where it is stored for use by the RAG/KB and GHL components. 

![graph TD    %% Define styles    classDef source fill:\#f8d7da,stroke:\#dc3545,stroke-width:2px,color:black;    classDef processing fill:\#d4edda,stroke:\#28a745,stroke-width:2px,color:black;    classDef storage fill:\#cce5ff,stroke:\#007bff,stroke-width:2px,color:black;    classDef utilization fill:\#fff3cd,stroke:\#ffc107,stroke-width:2px,color:black;    %% External Data Source    Auctions\[County Auctions\]:::source    %% The System Boundary    subgraph Surplus\_System \[The Surplus System Architecture\]                %% Components        WS\["Web Scraping Component (WS)\<br/\>(Performs Skip Tracing)"\]:::processing        AND\[("(AND) API & Database\<br/\>(Stores for Use)")\]:::storage        AR\_KB\[("(RAG/KB) Agentic RAG\<br/\>& Knowledge Base")\]:::utilization        GHL\["(GHL) GoHighLevel"\]:::utilization                %% Internal Data Flow        WS ==\>|"Hands over extracted\<br/\>skip tracing data"| AND        AND --\>|"Provides stored data"| AR\_KB        AND --\>|"Provides stored data"| GHL    end    %% External Connection    Auctions -.-\>|"Target for\<br/\>Data Collection"| WS][image7]  
*Figure 1: High level diagram of the Surplus Funds system*

All these components are what defines the Surplus Application.

## **Web Scraping Component**

This is where the whole process starts, with client acquisition (CA). Most auction data is readily available on auction portals in most counties. Those contain crucial information such as the property owner’s full name, contact details, surplus funds, and many more. That is where Surplus Funds Acquisition (SFA) agents usually start to acquire their clients. This is also where web scraping technologies can be implemented to automatically extract data instead of manually noting down details by hand. 

Uploading and updating data into the database is the only integration concern of the web scraping component. In this sense, this component has the easiest time integrating into the Surplus application. This also allows this component to focus solely on itself.

![flowchart LR    A\[Web Scraper\] --\> B\[Database\]    B --\> C\[Surplus Application\]    subgraph Scraper Scope        A    end    subgraph Core System        B        C    end][image8]  
*Figure 2: Web Scraper integration*

While web scraping can automate data extraction, it is not possible to create a general purpose web scraper that can extract data from any auction portal. For this reason, a dedicated web scraper must be developed for each auction portal. Not only that, auction portals may also change over time, requiring each web scraper to be tracked and kept up to date with those changes. Therefore, the web scraping component faces two challenges: horizontal scaling and maintenance.

![flowchart TD    subgraph Scaling Challenge        A1\[Multiple Auction Portals\]        A2\[One Scraper per Portal\]        A3\[Growing Number of Scrapers\]        A1 --\> A2 --\> A3    end    subgraph Maintenance Challenge        B1\[Portal Changes Over Time\]        B2\[Scrapers Break\]        B3\[Continuous Updates Required\]        B1 --\> B2 --\> B3    end    A3 --\> B3][image9]  
*Figure 3: Web Scraping challenges*

## **API & Database Component**

This component is responsible for managing lead/client information. This includes their information from the auction portals, supporting information, status, and etc. 

As each component of the Surplus application connects to the database for information storage and retrieval, it is also the component that glues the whole application together. In turn, this makes the AND component the more complex component to integrate.

![flowchart LR    WS\[Web Scraping\] --\>|Ingests Data| AND\[API & Database\]    ARKB\[Agentic RAG / KB\] \<--\>|Query & Update| AND    GHL\[GoHighLevel\] \<--\>|Query & Update| AND    subgraph AND Responsibilities        D1\[Data Storage\]        D2\[Data Validation\]        D3\[Access Control\]        D4\[Status Management\]    end    AND --- D1    AND --- D2    AND --- D3    AND --- D4][image10]  
*Figure 4: API & Database integration*

The primary concern of the AND component is to ensure that the data is easily sent, retrieved, updated, and tracked. Proper design of SQL tables is a must.

## **GoHighLevel Component**

The Customer Relationship Management (CRM) of the Surplus application. This component handles the execution and workflow of the Surplus application

It works by receiving qualified leads from the AND component and then calling RAG/KB endpoints for leveraging AI tools when interacting with leads/clients. While it stores data locally, the one source of truth should be the database in the AND component. Therefore, the GHL component should send back data about the status of each lead/client into the AND component.

![flowchart TB    subgraph Data\_Layer        AND\["API & Database\<br/\>(Source of Truth)"\]    end    subgraph Orchestration\_Layer        GHL\["CRM / Workflow Engine\<br/\>GoHighLevel"\]    end    subgraph Decision\_Layer        ARKB\["Agentic RAG / Knowledge Base\<br/\>AI Decision Engine"\]    end    subgraph Execution\_Layer        SMS\["SMS - DropCowboy"\]        CALL\["Voice Calls - Retell AI + ElevenLabs"\]        EMAIL\["Email - GHL Native"\]    end    AND --\>|Qualified Leads| GHL    GHL --\>|Request Strategy| ARKB    ARKB --\>|Message + Channel + Timing| GHL    GHL --\> SMS    GHL --\> CALL    GHL --\> EMAIL    SMS --\>|Replies| GHL    CALL --\>|Call Results| GHL    EMAIL --\>|Replies| GHL    GHL --\>|Interaction Data| ARKB    GHL --\>|Status Updates & Logs| AND][image11]  
*Figure 5: GoHighLevel integration*

Another aspect of the GHL component is its function to develop websites quickly and easily using its built in tools. The website will serve to inform leads/clients about the operations of Surplus Funds Acquisition.

## **Agentic RAG/Knowledge Base**

This component handles preparation of context aware information about the Surplus application. It is supplied with manuals, protocols, and other documents about and related to business operations which it can reference when prompted.

# Git & Github Guidelines

# **Github Guidelines**

#### **Github Branch Format**

| `<branch-type>/<branch-name>-#<ticket-tag>` |
| :---- |

#### All characters should be lowercase. Use kebab case for spaces (ex. feature/task-one-\#F001)

#### **Branch Types**

1. **feature**  
   - For feature implementations  
2. **bug**  
   - For bug fixing  
3. **refactor**  
   - For reimplementing features  
4. **doc**  
   - For documentation

#### **PR Guidelines**

1. Create a branch from the correct base branch.  
2. **Link the branch to the related GitHub issue.**  
3. Implement changes and push commits.  
4. Create a PR targeting the Develop branch   
5. **Link PR to issue**  
6. **Move issue to “For Review.”**  
7. Address review feedback if needed and repeat.   
   1. There will only be a **maximum of 2 PR cycles.**   
   2. After the 2nd PR cycle, it will be merged into develop and the DATL will align the feature to specification if needed.  
8. Merge upon approval and update issue status.

Welcome to the Metawatt Scrum Handbook. As we scale the Surplus Project with our 20 plus talented developers across 3 distinct teams, effective project management is our key to maximizing productivity and delivering high-quality AI-driven solutions.

**Core Metawatt Philosophy:** In this project, *every* developer undergoes a 3-day Scrum training. At the end of this period, one designated developer per team will officially assume the Scrum Master role. However, **any developer can (and should) act as the Scrum Master if the designated person is absent.** You are all equipped to lead, track, and unblock your teams.

***Fun Fact:*** The word Scrum comes from the sport of rugby, specifically as a shortened version of "scrummage".

![][image14]

## **1\. Scrum Terms and Definitions** {#1.-scrum-terms-and-definitions}

Before diving into the workflows, align yourself with the standard Metawatt terminology. This terminology applies regardless of the project management software we use.

* **Sprint:** A fixed, time-boxed period (usually 1–2 weeks) during which a specific, usable, and potentially releasable product increment is created.  
* **Backlog:** The master list of all tasks, features, and requirements needed for the project.  
* **Sprint Backlog:** The specific subset of Backlog items selected by the team to be completed during the current Sprint.  
* **Scrum Master (SM):** A servant-leader who facilitates Scrum events, removes blockers, and ensures the team follows agile practices.  
* **Blocker / Impediment:** Any issue, technical or organizational, that prevents a developer from completing their assigned task.  
* **Ticket / Issue:** A single unit of work on the team's project board.  
* **Kanban / Scrum Board:** The visual representation of work phases (e.g., *To Do*, *In Progress*, *In Review*, *Done*).  
* **Increment:** The sum of all the completed tasks and code merged at the end of a Sprint.  
* **Velocity:** A measure of the amount of work a Team can tackle during a single Sprint.  
* **Scrum of Scrums (Leadership Alignment Meeting):** A sync meeting where Team Scrum Masters meet with the Team Leads (Benny, Joerock, Dave) to coordinate cross-team dependencies and align on the roadmap.

## **2\. Metawatt Team Structure & Roles** {#2.-metawatt-team-structure-&-roles}

Because we are working with AI solutions, Agentic RAGs, and Web Scraping infrastructure, cross-team collaboration is critical.

### **Organizational Flow** {#organizational-flow}

* **Leadership Team (Product Owners & Tech Vision)**  
  * Dave Angelo Jimenez — API & Database  
  * Benny Gil — Agentic RAG / Knowledge Graph  
  * Joerock Valleseran — Web Scraping  
* **Development Teams (Self-Managing Execution)**  
  * **Team 1:** API & DB (6-7 Developers, 1 Scrum Master)  
  * **Team 2:** RAG (6-7 Developers, 1 Scrum Master)  
  * **Team 3:** Scraping (6-7 Developers, 1 Scrum Master)  
* **Communication Bridge:** The 3 Scrum Masters meet 1-2x weekly with the Leadership Team for alignment and cross-team dependency resolution.

### **The Roles** {#the-roles}

* **The Developers:** Self-managing professionals who turn the Sprint Backlog into a working Increment. You estimate your own work, pick up tickets, and collaborate.  
* **The Scrum Master:** The designated tracker and facilitator. If the SM is absent, **any developer** steps in to run the Daily Scrum and update the board.  
* **The Team Leads (Dave, Benny, Joerock):** Acting as the Product Owners/Stakeholders. They prioritize the master backlog, accept completed work, and define the technical vision.

![][image15]

## **3\. The Metawatt Sprint Lifecycle** {#3.-the-metawatt-sprint-lifecycle}

The Scrum framework relies on a predictable rhythm. Below is the lifecycle of a standard Metawatt Sprint.

![][image16]

### **Phase 1: Sprint Start** {#phase-1:-sprint-start}

1. **Prioritization:** Team Leads prioritize the Master Backlog.  
2. **Sprint Planning:** The Team and Team Leads agree on the Sprint Goal. Developers pull tickets into their Sprint Backlog, estimating effort and explicitly flagging any dependencies on other teams.

### **Phase 2: Daily Execution** {#phase-2:-daily-execution}

1. **Daily Scrum (15 Mins Max):** A quick standup where each developer answers:  
   * *What did I accomplish yesterday?*  
   * *What will I work on today?*  
   * *Are there any blockers in my way?* *(Note: Do not solve deep technical problems here. Take them to a separate discussion right after the meeting).*  
2. **Board Updates & Unblocking:** Scrum Master updates the board and acts immediately to remove any raised blockers.

### **Phase 3: Cross-Team Sync** {#phase-3:-cross-team-sync}

1. **Leadership Alignment Meeting (1-2x Weekly):** Scrum Masters meet with Dave, Benny, and Joerock to report velocity, highlight cross-team dependencies, and align for upcoming sprints.

### **Phase 4: Sprint End** {#phase-4:-sprint-end}

1. **Sprint Review:** The team demos working software/completed tickets to the Team Leads.  
2. **Sprint Retrospective:** Internal team meeting to discuss what went well, what went wrong, and process improvements for the next Sprint.

## **4\. Software-Agnostic Board Management** {#4.-software-agnostic-board-management}

Whether Metawatt uses GitHub Projects, ClickUp, or any other PM software, the rules of board management remain exactly the same.

1. **State Representation:** Every ticket must accurately reflect its current state.  
   * **To Do:** Work planned for the sprint but not started.  
   * **In Progress:** Work currently being tackled by a developer. *(Limit work-in-progress to avoid context switching\!)*  
   * **In Review:** Code completed but awaiting a pull request review or QA testing. *(Note: Per Metawatt Guidelines, a maximum of 2 PR cycles are allowed before merging to develop).*  
   * **Done:** Fully merged, tested, and accepted.  
2. **Ticket Hygiene:** A ticket is not valid unless it has:  
   * A clear title and description.  
   * An assignee (who is doing the work).  
   * Acceptance criteria (how do we know it is "Done"?).  
   * A direct link to the associated GitHub branch and Pull Request.  
3. **Flagging Blockers:** If a developer is stuck, the ticket must be visibly flagged (using tags, labels, or a specific "Blocked" column) so the Scrum Master can immediately spot it and take action.

## **5\. The Scrum Master Checklists** {#5.-the-scrum-master-checklists}

Use these checklists to guide your daily and weekly responsibilities. Remember, if you are stepping in for an absent Scrum Master, simply pick up this list.

### **Daily Checklist** {#daily-checklist}

- [ ] **Review the Board:** Before the Daily Scrum, check the board. Are there tickets sitting in "In Progress" for too long? Are any tickets missing assignees?  
- [ ] **Facilitate Daily Scrum:** Ensure the meeting starts on time, stays under 15 minutes, and prevents developers from rambling into deep technical debates.  
- [ ] **Unblock the Team:** Identify any blockers raised during the standup and immediately coordinate with other teams or Team Leads to resolve them.  
- [ ] **Stakeholder Transparency:** Ensure the current board state accurately reflects reality so Dave, Benny, and Joerock can view project health asynchronously.

### **Weekly / Sprint Checklist** {#weekly-/-sprint-checklist}

- [ ] **Prep the Backlog:** Ensure the backlog is prioritized and tickets are well-defined before Sprint Planning.  
- [ ] **Facilitate the Retrospective:** Create a safe space for developers to voice process frustrations and celebrate wins.  
- [ ] **Attend Leadership Alignment:** Come prepared to the meeting with Dave, Benny, and Joerock. Bring data: What is the team's velocity? What are the biggest risks? What cross-team support do you need?

*“Great Scrum is not about rigidly following rules; it is about building a framework that allows brilliant developers to communicate, self-correct, and ship great software.” — Yours truly*

The era of writing every line of code manually is ending. Today, the most effective developers operate as orchestrators, guiding autonomous AI agents to build, test, and debug software. This guide focuses entirely on the practical application of AI in software engineering. This framework provides the exact workflows, configuration setups, and tool knowledge needed to integrate AI coding assistants into your daily development cycle without sacrificing code quality.

## **1\. The Core Rules of Agentic Coding** {#1.-the-core-rules-of-agentic-coding}

To successfully use an AI coding agent, you must fundamentally change how you interact with your tools. Treat your AI not as a senior mentor, but as an exceptionally fast, highly capable junior engineer who requires clear boundaries, strict instructions, and careful supervision.

### **Manage Your Context (The Agent's Memory)** {#manage-your-context-(the-agent's-memory)}

An AI's "context window" is its short-term memory. It holds your prompt, the files it has read, and the output it generates. It is a finite resource. If you flood the context window with too much irrelevant code, the AI will "forget" your original instructions and start making mistakes.

![][image17]

*Figure 1: The Context Window Architecture*

**Understanding the Diagram:**

To manage your agent effectively, you must understand the difference between Static and Dynamic context.

* **Static Context** contains the foundational rules of your project (like your CLAUDE.md file). Because this data rarely changes, the AI system caches it, making it extremely fast and cheap to process.  
* **Dynamic Context** builds up as you chat with the AI. Every time the agent reads a new file, runs a command, or outputs a terminal log, it fills up this layer.  
* **The Trap:** Tool outputs (like a massive error stack trace from a failed test) are the biggest cause of "context rot." If the dynamic context gets too bloated, it pushes out the AI's ability to focus on your original goal.  
* **The Solution:** Use progressive disclosure. Don't dump your whole repository into the prompt. Give the agent lightweight file paths and let it load data only when needed. If the agent gets confused, clear the chat and start a fresh session to wipe the dynamic context clean.

## **2\. The Agentic Coding Cookbook: Proven Workflows** {#2.-the-agentic-coding-cookbook:-proven-workflows}

Do not sit down and simply ask an AI to "build a feature." Instead, follow these structured, industry-proven workflows to ensure your agent builds exactly what you need.

### **Workflow 1: Spec-Driven Development (SDD)** {#workflow-1:-spec-driven-development-(sdd)}

Before you allow the AI to generate a single line of code, write a `spec.md` document. This forces you to think through the architecture and gives the AI a definitive source of truth to refer back to. A good spec includes:

* **Objective:** What are we building?  
* **Tech Stack:** Exactly which languages, frameworks, and versions.  
* **Commands:** How to build (`npm run build`), test (`npm test`), and lint the project.  
* **Boundaries:** Explicit rules like "Always run tests before commits," "Never commit secrets," or "Ask before modifying database schemas."

Notable Agentic Toolkits for SDD: 

* OpenSpec ([https://github.com/Fission-AI/OpenSpec](https://github.com/Fission-AI/OpenSpec))  
* SpecKit ([https://github.com/github/spec-kit](https://github.com/github/spec-kit))

### **Workflow 2: The Plan-Act-Reflect Loop** {#workflow-2:-the-plan-act-reflect-loop}

Prevent your agent from rushing into writing code and making assumptions by enforcing a strict operational loop:

![][image18]

*Figure 2: The Plan-Act-Reflect AI Governance Loop*

**Understanding the Diagram:**

This flowchart illustrates the critical boundary between human oversight and autonomous AI execution.

* **The Planning Gate (Yellow):** The agent must always stop and ask for your approval after drafting a plan. As a developer, reviewing the agent's plan helps you catch architectural mistakes *before* it generates thousands of lines of messy code.  
* **The Execution Sub-loop (Blue/Red):** Once you approve the plan, the agent enters a self-correcting loop. It writes code, runs the tests you defined in your `spec.md`, and reads the terminal output. If the tests fail, it automatically loops back to analyze the stack trace and fix its own code without needing you to copy-paste the errors.

### **Workflow 3: Agentic Debugging** {#workflow-3:-agentic-debugging}

When a bug occurs in production or during testing, do not blindly paste the error stack trace into the AI and ask for a fix.

1. **Reason First, Then Act:** Force the AI to explain its understanding of the data flow and the root cause *before* you allow it to generate a code patch.  
2. **Add Logging:** Ask the AI to inject `console.log` or debug statements into the code first, run the app, and feed the actual runtime logs back to the agent.  
3. **Keep State Clean:** If the agent fails to fix the bug after a few tries, the context is likely polluted. Start a brand new chat session with a clean context to try again.

### **Workflow 4: Version Control and Code Review** {#workflow-4:-version-control-and-code-review}

The golden rule of agentic coding: AI agents can propose code, but they never own it.

* **Draft PRs Only:** Configure your agent to only open draft Pull Requests. Never allow an AI to push directly to main or production branches.  
* **Mandatory Human Review:** Treat the agent's PR exactly as you would a human's. Review the logic, check for edge cases, and ensure security (e.g., input validation, auth logic) is intact.

## **3\. Harness Engineering: Setting Up Your Workspace** {#3.-harness-engineering:-setting-up-your-workspace}

Harness engineering is the practice of designing the rules and environments that govern your AI. Instead of repeating your preferences in every prompt, you anchor your project with a persistent configuration file.

### **The `CLAUDE.md` / `AGENTS.md` File** {#the-claude.md-/-agents.md-file}

Create a `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md` file in the root of your repository. This acts as the agent's permanent memory and system prompt for the project.

* **Keep it brief:** Aim for under 200 lines to save on token costs and ensure the AI reads it carefully.  
* **Make it corrective, not just descriptive:** Don't just describe the project. Use this file to enforce rules based on past mistakes. For example: "Always use forward slashes for file paths on Windows," or "Never auto-commit code; ask for explicit permission first."

## **4\. Expanding Your Toolkit: MCPs and Open Source Agents** {#4.-expanding-your-toolkit:-mcps-and-open-source-agents}

To effectively orchestrate AI, you need to understand the tools at your disposal and how to extend them.

### **The Model Context Protocol (MCP)** {#the-model-context-protocol-(mcp)}

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) acts as a universal adapter, giving your AI agent "hands" to interact with external systems—reading files, querying databases, searching the web, or managing your GitHub repository.

![][image19]Figure 3: MCP Handshake and Data Flow

**Understanding the Diagram:**

This sequence shows exactly how an agent interacts with the outside world securely.

* **Discovery Phase (tools/list):** When you ask a question, your IDE/Client first asks the local MCP Server what tools it has available. The server replies with schemas (like a blueprint) explaining how to use its tools.  
* **Execution Phase (tools/call):** The LLM decides which tool to use based on the schema, but it does *not* execute it directly. The Host Application tells the MCP Server to run the tool, fetching the data from the external source.  
* **Injection:** The raw data is returned to the Host, which injects it into the LLM's context window so the AI can read it and formulate a natural language answer for you.

**Essential MCP Servers to explore:**

* **GitHub MCP:** Allows your agent to read open issues, review PRs, and manage your repository autonomously.  
* **Playwright / Browserbase:** Enables the agent to control a headless browser, visually inspect UI changes, and run end-to-end tests.  
* **Context7:** Connects to up-to-date developer documentation so your AI doesn't hallucinate outdated syntax or APIs.  
* **Code-Review-Graph:** A Python tool that parses your codebase into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) using Tree-sitter and stores it in a local SQLite database. It exposes this structural graph to your AI assistant via MCP. Instead of grepping through individual files—which wastes massive amounts of tokens—your agent can directly query the graph for structural questions like "what calls this function?" or "what is the blast radius of this change?". This approach can reduce token consumption by up to 120x on large tasks.  
* **Graphify:** Similar to code-review-graph, Graphify exposes your codebase graph as a set of LLM-callable tools. It provides your autonomous agents with structured, deep codebase understanding rather than restricting them to simple file search algorithms.

### **Comparative Analysis of Major AI Coding Tools** {#comparative-analysis-of-major-ai-coding-tools}

Understanding the structural philosophies of different tools helps you pick the right one for the job.

| Feature Dimension | GitHub Copilot | Claude Code | Google Antigravity |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **Primary Interface Architecture** | Editor Extension integrated directly into existing IDEs (e.g., VS Code). | Command-Line Interface (CLI) application operating via the terminal. | Standalone, Agent-First IDE application featuring dual Manager and Editor interfaces. |
| **Execution Autonomy Level** | Medium. Generates sophisticated suggestions but relies on manual human orchestration. | High. Full autonomous access to the terminal to execute agentic loops and run tests. | High. Enforces Planning and Execution loops. Capable of autonomous visual testing via a built-in browser. |
| **Best For** | Developers needing inline syntax help and targeted assistance within a familiar IDE. | Developers needing deep reasoning for repetitive, multi-step engineering backlogs across the terminal. | Teams prioritizing architectural planning and persistent, version-controlled markdown artifacts. |

*Note: The open-source community also offers powerful, free alternatives like **Aider** (a terminal-first git-native agent), **Pi** (a minimalist and unopinionated coding tool), and **Cline** (an agentic assistant integrating directly into VS Code).*

## **Conclusion** {#conclusion}

Agentic coding is not about letting an AI do your job; it is about elevating your role from a syntax-writer to a system architect. By mastering Spec-Driven Development, enforcing strict Plan-Act-Reflect loops, properly utilizing project configuration files like CLAUDE.md, and leveraging MCP tools, developers can safely and effectively harness the massive productivity gains of modern AI coding assistants.
